$doc: HOW THE GREAT POWERS STAND WITH EACH OTHER - the tariff half of a company's profit tax (docs/PRICE_FACTORS.md §3.2, F4/F5, slice P4; migration 0195).
note: The owner, 2026-10-18: 'is there a way for the prices move on many different factors? like relationship with other countries'. One row per UNORDERED pair of the ten great powers (public.great_powers, 0187) that is NOT at peace; every pair not listed is at peace. The stance multiplies the profit tax a company of one power pays in a city the other holds (world.tax_rate): ally x0.5, rival x1.5, war x2 (knob tariff_stance_mult), never above tariff_rate_max 35 %. Authored, not simulated (F5): the stances of the years 1580-1640 that the histories agree on, each defended in a line. NOT the owner's - confirm every row.

relations.why: the Treaty of Windsor (1386), the oldest alliance in Europe, held through the century
the Iberian Union (1580-1640): one king in Madrid and Lisbon
the Treaty of Nonsuch (1585): England sent an army to the Dutch revolt against Spain
the Franco-Ottoman alliance and the capitulations of 1536 lowered French customs in the Levant
Joseon was Ming's tributary, and Ming armies fought for it in the Imjin War (1592-98)
the Anglo-Spanish War (1585-1604) and the Armada of 1588
Habsburg against Valois and Bourbon, from the Italian Wars to the war of 1635
the Habsburg-Ottoman wars for the Mediterranean: Tunis, Malta, Lepanto (1571)
the Ottoman-Portuguese wars for the Indian Ocean, Diu (1538) to Hormuz
the wokou raids and Ming's ban on trade with Japan; Ming fought Japan in Korea
the Imjin War (1592-98); trade reopened only by the Treaty of Giyu (1609)
the Eighty Years' War (1568-1648), the Dutch revolt against the Spanish crown
the Dutch-Portuguese War (1602-1663) for the spice trade, from Malacca to Brazil
